name: Head crest
function: Most likely display: signalling species, age or maturity to other pterosaurs.

name: Toothless beak
function: Catching food. Many researchers think it stalked on the ground like a giant stork, snapping up small animals; other feeding ideas are still debated.

name: Long neck
function: Reaching down to the ground for food while standing on all fours.

name: Pteroid bone
function: It supported the small front membrane (propatagium). Angling it changed the wing's leading edge, helping to control lift at low speed.

name: Wing finger
function: Holding the outer membrane taut in flight; it folded away when the animal walked.

name: Hind limb
function: Walking, and the first push at take-off. Most researchers think giant pterosaurs launched on all fours, vaulting into the air mainly with their strong arms.

name: Skull
function: Houses the brain and the senses; its length makes room for the long rows of cheek teeth.

name: High-crowned teeth
function: Grinding tough plant food for many years without wearing out.

name: Three-toed foot
function: Support and grip; the side toes probably touched the ground only on soft footing or at speed – still being studied.

name: Cannon bone
function: A light lever that lengthens the stride for fast running.

name: Spine and withers
function: Carries the body between the limbs and lets the horse lower its head to graze without effort.

name: Hind limb
function: The main engine for running: the hind legs push the body forward.

name: Arched upper jaw
function: Makes room for the baleen plates, which in right whales can be over two metres long.

name: Lower jaw
function: With the lips they scoop around the baleen while the whale skims the water with its mouth open.

name: Flipper
function: Steering and balance; the tail does the pushing.

name: Ribs
function: Protect heart and lungs while letting the chest compress during dives.

name: Pelvic remnant
function: No longer used for walking; they anchor muscles of the reproductive organs.

name: Tail vertebrae
function: Muscles along these vertebrae drive the up-and-down stroke that powers swimming.
